title: Which step to speed?
hook: A reaction runs in two steps. Make one of them ten times faster. Does it matter which?

knows: that rate constants set how fast one step goes (multiply-dont-add-rates, the-slowing-half-life)
doesNotKnow: that in a chain of steps the slowest step sets the overall time, so speeding up a fast step barely helps

misconception: Making any step of a reaction faster speeds the whole reaction up in proportion.
objective: The learner can say that speeding the fast step of A → B → C tenfold barely moves the half-time (7.03 s to 6.94 s) while speeding the slow step tenfold cuts it to 0.80 s, and explain that the slowest step sets the pace (the rate-determining step).

claims.text: For consecutive first-order steps A → B → C starting from pure A, the fraction of A turned into C is 1 − (k2 e^(−k1 t) − k1 e^(−k2 t))/(k2 − k1) (the curves drawn on the stage).
claims.source: Integrating d[A]/dt = −k1[A], d[B]/dt = k1[A] − k2[B], [C] = [A]0 − [A] − [B] (Atkins & de Paula, Physical Chemistry, consecutive elementary reactions). Demo.tsx C(). Brief claim 1.
claims.note: Derivation: the closed form checked against my own RK4 integration of dA/dt = -k1 A, dB/dt = k1 A - k2 B. The half-times agree to 4 decimals for all four (k1, k2) pairs. Atkins not needed.

claims.text: With k1 = 0.1 /s and k2 = 10 /s, half the C appears at 7.03 s; with k2 = 100 /s, at 6.94 s; with k1 = 1 /s and k2 = 10 /s, at 0.80 s; with both sped up, at 0.70 s (stage legend 'start: 7.03 s', 'step 2 ×10: 6.94 s', 'step 1 ×10: 0.80 s', 'both ×10: 0.70 s'; reveal: 'from 7.03 s to 6.94 s', 'cut it to 0.80 s'; right option 'almost no sooner').
claims.source: The lesson's own bisection on the closed form of claim 1 (Demo.tsx halfTime(), 100 halvings of [0, 100] s), re-run in node by demo-builder 2026-10-14: 7.032, 6.941, 0.798, 0.703 s. 7.03 / 6.94 = 1.01 (1% sooner). Brief claim 2.
claims.note: Re-run in node with my own copies of C() and halfTime() and an independent RK4: 7.0320, 6.9415, 0.7984 and 0.7032 s, shown as 7.03, 6.94, 0.80 and 0.70 s. 7.03/6.94 = 1.013, so 'almost no sooner' is right.

claims.text: When one step is much slower than the rest, it sets the pace of the whole reaction: the rate-determining step (reveal: 'the slowest step sets the pace of the whole reaction. That step is the rate-determining step').
claims.source: Atkins & de Paula, Physical Chemistry, the rate-determining step; claim 2 shows it numerically (with k2 ≫ k1 the half-time approaches ln 2 / k1 = 6.93 s).
claims.note: Derivation: as k2/k1 -> infinity, C(t) -> 1 - exp(-k1 t), and the half-time -> ln 2/k1 = 6.93 s; c2 shows it numerically. 'Rate-determining step' is the name of this limit (terminology). No outside fact rests on Atkins.

claims.text: Model disclosure: the rate constants (0.1 /s and 10 /s) are illustrative, not a real reaction (question: 'Step 1 is slow; step 2 is 100 times faster').
claims.source: The lesson's own model (brief claim 4); the gate openings on the stage grow with log k and are a picture, not a measurement.
claims.note: Convention, consistent: k1 = 0.1 /s and k2 = 10 /s match the question's 'step 2 is 100 times faster'; no real reaction is named.

claims.text: The rate-determining step is the one a catalyst, or a chemist, has to speed up to make the whole reaction faster (reveal); molecules queue at the narrowest gate (reveal, a picture of A waiting before the slow step).
claims.source: Follows from claims 2-3: only a change to the slow step's rate constant moves the half-time much. General statement in Atkins & de Paula (catalysis lowers the barrier of the rate-limiting step). The 'queue' image: with k2 ≫ k1, B stays tiny and the material waits as A.
claims.note: Derivation within the model: only a change to k1 moves the half-time much (7.03 -> 0.80 s, against 7.03 -> 6.94 s). With k2 >> k1, B stays tiny and material waits as A (the 'queue'). The general remark about catalysts is not used as evidence.

recall.question: A three-step process has steps taking about 1 s, 1 s and 60 s on average. You can make one step 10 times faster. Which choice speeds up the whole process the most?
options: Any one of them, it is the same
recall.why: The slowest step sets the pace of a chain. Speeding up a fast step barely changes the total; speeding up the slow one is what helps (the rate-determining step).
